claim: C. elegans mounts transcriptional defense responses against intestinal bacterial infections that elicit overlapping starvation and infection responses.
source: The model organism Caenorhabditis elegans mounts transcriptional defense responses against intestinal bacterial infections that elicit overlapping starvation and infection responses, the regulation of which is not well understood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background context for the study.

claim: Direct comparison of C. elegans that were starved or infected with Staphylococcus aureus revealed a large infection-specific transcriptional signature.
source: Direct comparison of C. elegans that were starved or infected with Staphylococcus aureus revealed a large infection-specific transcriptional signature, which was almost completely abrogated by deletion of transcription factor hlh-30/TFEB, except for six genes including a flavin-containing monooxygenase (FMO) gene, fmo-2/FMO5.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The infection-specific transcriptional signature was almost completely abrogated by deletion of transcription factor hlh-30/TFEB, except for six genes including fmo-2/FMO5.
source: Direct comparison of C. elegans that were starved or infected with Staphylococcus aureus revealed a large infection-specific transcriptional signature, which was almost completely abrogated by deletion of transcription factor hlh-30/TFEB, except for six genes including a flavin-containing monooxygenase (FMO) gene, fmo-2/FMO5.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data comparing wild type and hlh-30 mutants under starvation and infection conditions.

claim: Deletion of fmo-2/FMO5 severely compromised infection survival.
source: Deletion of fmo-2/FMO5 severely compromised infection survival, thus identifying the first FMO with innate immunity functions in animals.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: fmo-2/FMO5 is the first FMO with innate immunity functions in animals.
source: Deletion of fmo-2/FMO5 severely compromised infection survival, thus identifying the first FMO with innate immunity functions in animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and stated explicitly in the abstract.

claim: fmo-2/FMO5 induction required the nuclear hormone receptor NHR-49/PPAR-α.
source: Moreover, fmo-2/FMO5 induction required the nuclear hormone receptor, NHR-49/PPAR-α, which controlled host defense cell non-autonomously.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RT-qPCR and fluorescence microscopy data in Figure 3.

claim: NHR-49/PPAR-α controlled host defense cell non-autonomously.
source: Moreover, fmo-2/FMO5 induction required the nuclear hormone receptor, NHR-49/PPAR-α, which controlled host defense cell non-autonomously.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by tissue-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: HLH-30/TFEB is the main regulator of the infection-specific host response to S. aureus.
source: These findings reveal an infection-specific host response to S. aureus, identify HLH-30/TFEB as its main regulator, reveal FMOs as important innate immunity effectors in animals, and identify the mechanism of FMO regulation through NHR-49/PPAR-α during S. aureus infection, with implications for host defense and inflammation in higher organisms.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by RNA-seq data showing that hlh-30 deletion abrogates most of the infection-specific signature.

claim: FMOs are important innate immunity effectors in animals.
source: These findings reveal an infection-specific host response to S. aureus, identify HLH-30/TFEB as its main regulator, reveal FMOs as important innate immunity effectors in animals, and identify the mechanism of FMO regulation through NHR-49/PPAR-α during S. aureus infection, with implications for host defense and inflammation in higher organisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that fmo-2 deletion compromises infection survival.

claim: C. elegans feed on microbes that grow on rotting vegetable matter in their natural habitat.
source: In their natural habitat, C. elegans feed on microbes that grow on rotting vegetable matter, and thus face a high likelihood of ingesting pathogens (Schulenburg and Félix, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schulenburg and Félix, 2017.

claim: C. elegans face a high likelihood of ingesting pathogens in their natural habitat.
source: In their natural habitat, C. elegans feed on microbes that grow on rotting vegetable matter, and thus face a high likelihood of ingesting pathogens (Schulenburg and Félix, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schulenburg and Félix, 2017.

claim: C. elegans possess innate host defense mechanisms that promote their survival.
source: To defend against infection, C. elegans possess innate host defense mechanisms that promote their survival (Ermolaeva and Schumacher, 2014; Kim and Ewbank, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ermolaeva and Schumacher, 2014 and Kim and Ewbank, 2018.

claim: Model human pathogenic bacteria cause intestinal pathology and death in C. elegans through poorly understood mechanisms.
source: In the laboratory, model human pathogenic bacteria cause intestinal pathology and death through poorly understood mechanisms (Irazoqui et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Irazoqui et al., 2010a.

claim: C. elegans gene expression changes in response to pathogenic bacteria, fungi, and viruses are mounted through evolutionarily conserved mechanisms.
source: Over the last 15 years, several studies have identified and characterized C. elegans gene expression changes in response to pathogenic bacteria, fungi, and viruses, mounted through evolutionarily conserved mechanisms (Irazoqui et al., 2010b; Kim and Ewbank, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Irazoqui et al., 2010b and Kim and Ewbank, 2018.

claim: Ingested Gram-positive bacterium Staphylococcus aureus causes drastic cytopathology in C. elegans.
source: We previously showed that ingested Gram-positive bacterium Staphylococcus aureus causes drastic cytopathology in C. elegans (Irazoqui et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Irazoqui et al., 2010a.

claim: Infection with S. aureus results in progressive effacement and lysis of intestinal epithelial cells, whole-body cellular breakdown, and death.
source: Infection with S. aureus results in progressive effacement and lysis of intestinal epithelial cells, whole-body cellular breakdown, and death (Irazoqui et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Irazoqui et al., 2010a.

claim: C. elegans mount a pathogen-specific transcriptional host response against S. aureus, which includes genes that encode antimicrobial proteins and cytoprotective factors.
source: In previous work, we showed that C. elegans mount a pathogen-specific transcriptional host response against S. aureus, which includes genes that encode antimicrobial proteins (e.g. lysozymes, antimicrobial peptides, and secreted C-type lectins) and cytoprotective factors (e.g. autophagy genes, lysosomal factors, and chaperones) that are necessary and sufficient for survival (Irazoqui et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Irazoqui et al., 2010a.

claim: Antimicrobial proteins and cytoprotective factors induced by S. aureus infection are necessary and sufficient for survival.
source: In previous work, we showed that C. elegans mount a pathogen-specific transcriptional host response against S. aureus, which includes genes that encode antimicrobial proteins (e.g. lysozymes, antimicrobial peptides, and secreted C-type lectins) and cytoprotective factors (e.g. autophagy genes, lysosomal factors, and chaperones) that are necessary and sufficient for survival (Irazoqui et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Irazoqui et al., 2010a.

claim: C. elegans still induced select host defense genes even when exposed to heat-killed S. aureus, which did not cause intestinal destruction.
source: Moreover, we discovered that C. elegans still induced select host defense genes even when exposed to heat-killed S. aureus, which did not cause intestinal destruction (Irazoqui et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Irazoqui et al., 2010a.

claim: The induction of a large majority of the transcriptional host response to S. aureus requires HLH-30.
source: We recently discovered that the induction of a large majority of the transcriptional host response to S. aureus requires HLH-30, the C. elegans homolog of mammalian transcription factor EB (TFEB) (Visvikis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Visvikis et al., 2014.

claim: HLH-30 is the C. elegans homolog of mammalian transcription factor EB (TFEB).
source: We recently discovered that the induction of a large majority of the transcriptional host response to S. aureus requires HLH-30, the C. elegans homolog of mammalian transcription factor EB (TFEB) (Visvikis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Visvikis et al., 2014.

claim: TFEB belongs to the MiT family of transcription factors.
source: TFEB belongs to the MiT family of transcription factors, which in mammals and C. elegans controls the transcription of autophagy and lysosomal genes in response to nutritional stress in addition to infection (Lapierre et al., 2013; Raben and Puertollano, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lapierre et al., 2013 and Raben and Puertollano, 2016.

claim: The MiT family of transcription factors controls the transcription of autophagy and lysosomal genes in response to nutritional stress in addition to infection in mammals and C. elegans.
source: TFEB belongs to the MiT family of transcription factors, which in mammals and C. elegans controls the transcription of autophagy and lysosomal genes in response to nutritional stress in addition to infection (Lapierre et al., 2013; Raben and Puertollano, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lapierre et al., 2013 and Raben and Puertollano, 2016.

claim: HLH-30 and TFEB regulate lipid store mobilization during nutritional deprivation.
source: HLH-30 and TFEB also regulate lipid store mobilization during nutritional deprivation (O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013; Settembre et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013 and Settembre et al., 2013.

claim: 388 genes were differentially expressed between infected and starved animals.
source: We identified 388 genes that were differentially expressed between these two conditions (Figure 1B,C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B,C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: About 70% (283) of differentially expressed genes were upregulated by starvation.
source: About 70% (283) of differentially expressed genes were upregulated by starvation, while about 30% (105) were upregulated by infection (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RNA-seq data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: About 30% (105) of differentially expressed genes were upregulated by infection.
source: About 70% (283) of differentially expressed genes were upregulated by starvation, while about 30% (105) were upregulated by infection (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RNA-seq data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Starvation-induced genes belong mostly to metabolic processes.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis showed the starvation-induced genes to belong mostly to metabolic processes, whereas the infection-specific signature was highly enriched for innate immune response genes (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by GO analysis data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The infection-specific signature was highly enriched for innate immune response genes.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis showed the starvation-induced genes to belong mostly to metabolic processes, whereas the infection-specific signature was highly enriched for innate immune response genes (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by GO analysis data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: In hlh-30/TFEB mutants, differential gene expression between starvation and infection was almost completely abrogated.
source: To our surprise, in hlh-30/TFEB mutants differential gene expression between starvation and infection was almost completely abrogated (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Of the 105 genes in the infection-specific signature, only six were induced in hlh-30/TFEB mutants.
source: Of the 105 genes in the infection-specific signature, only six were induced in hlh-30/TFEB mutants (Figure 2B), including clec-52, fmo-2/FMO5, and the uncharacterized genes C33A12.19, C54F6.12, K08C7.4, and Y47H9C.1 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The six genes induced in hlh-30/TFEB mutants during infection include clec-52, fmo-2/FMO5, C33A12.19, C54F6.12, K08C7.4, and Y47H9C.1.
source: Of the 105 genes in the infection-specific signature, only six were induced in hlh-30/TFEB mutants (Figure 2B), including clec-52, fmo-2/FMO5, and the uncharacterized genes C33A12.19, C54F6.12, K08C7.4, and Y47H9C.1 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RNA-seq data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: fmo-2/FMO5 was partially induced in hlh-30/TFEB mutants compared to wild type.
source: Particularly, we verified that fmo-2/FMO5 was partially induced in hlh-30/TFEB mutants compared to wild type (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Partial induction of fmo-2/FMO5 in hlh-30/TFEB mutants was rescued by transgenic re-expression of hlh-30/TFEB driven by its endogenous promoter.
source: Partial induction of fmo-2/FMO5 in hlh-30/TFEB mutants was rescued by transgenic re-expression of hlh-30/TFEB driven by its endogenous promoter (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: HLH-30/TFEB is crucial for both the starvation and the infection-specific responses.
source: Altogether, these results showed that HLH-30/TFEB is crucial for both the starvation and the infection-specific responses, and hinted at an HLH-30/TFEB-independent pathway for the induction of six infection-specific genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq and RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 2.

claim: There is an HLH-30/TFEB-independent pathway for the induction of six infection-specific genes.
source: Altogether, these results showed that HLH-30/TFEB is crucial for both the starvation and the infection-specific responses, and hinted at an HLH-30/TFEB-independent pathway for the induction of six infection-specific genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that six genes are still induced in hlh-30 mutants during infection.

claim: fmo-2/FMO5 expression was induced several thousand-fold in S. aureus-infected animals relative to nonpathogenic E. coli controls.
source: As shown previously (Irazoqui et al., 2010a) fmo-2/FMO5 expression was induced several thousand-fold in S. aureus-infected animals relative to nonpathogenic E. coli controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, with a citation to Irazoqui et al., 2010a.

claim: Animals infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa exhibited no significant change in fmo-2/FMO5 expression.
source: In contrast, animals infected with Gram-negative pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa exhibited no significant change (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), consistent with previous results (Irazoqui et al., 2008; Irazoqui et al., 2010a; Wong et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, with citations to previous studies.

claim: S. aureus caused high GFP induction in all tissues, except in gonads and eggs, in the fmo-2/FMO5 transcriptional reporter.
source: In stark contrast, S. aureus caused high GFP induction in all tissues, except in gonads and eggs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: fmo-2/FMO5 is strongly induced in a pathogen-specific manner.
source: These observations confirmed that fmo-2/FMO5 is strongly induced in a pathogen-specific manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fluorescence microscopy and RT-qPCR data comparing different pathogens.

claim: Infection causes fmo-2/FMO5 induction independently of previously identified host defense pathways, including p38 MAPK, TGF-β, ERK, insulin, Wnt, and HIF-1 pathways.
source: Our prior studies also showed that infection causes fmo-2/FMO5 induction independently of previously identified host defense pathways, including p38 MAPK, TGF-β, ERK, insulin, Wnt, and HIF-1 pathways (Irazoqui et al., 2008; Irazoqui et al., 2010a; Luhachack et al., 2012; Visvikis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: fmo-2/FMO5 can be partially induced independently of HLH-30/TFEB.
source: Additionally, we found that fmo-2/FMO5 can be partially induced independently of HLH-30/TFEB (Figure 2 and Visvikis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2, with a citation to Visvikis et al., 2014.

claim: NHR-49, a nuclear receptor homologous to human PPAR-α and HNF4-α, is essential for fmo-2/FMO5 induction during exogenous oxidative stress.
source: Previous studies identified NHR-49, a nuclear receptor homologous to human PPAR-α and HNF4-α, as essential for fmo-2/FMO5 induction during exogenous oxidative stress (Goh et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goh et al., 2018 and Hu et al., 2018.

claim: In nhr-49/PPARA null mutants, expression of the fmo-2/FMO5 fluorescent transcriptional reporter was barely induced.
source: We found that in these mutants, expression of the fmo-2/FMO5 fluorescent transcriptional reporter was barely induced (Figure 3F,G) and, importantly, was undetectable in the intestinal epithelium (Figure 3H–K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3F,G,H-K.

claim: In nhr-49/PPARA null mutants, fmo-2/FMO5 expression was undetectable in the intestinal epithelium.
source: We found that in these mutants, expression of the fmo-2/FMO5 fluorescent transcriptional reporter was barely induced (Figure 3F,G) and, importantly, was undetectable in the intestinal epithelium (Figure 3H–K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3H-K.

claim: In hlh-30/TFEB mutants, fmo-2/FMO5 expression was preserved in the pharyngeal isthmus, pharyngeal-intestinal valve, and in the intestinal epithelium, albeit to lower levels compared to wild type.
source: In contrast, fmo-2/FMO5 induction by S. aureus was partially dependent on hlh-30/TFEB, as predicted by RNA-seq (Figure 3A–D and G, Figure 2); in these mutants, expression was preserved in the pharyngeal isthmus, pharyngeal-intestinal valve, and in the intestinal epithelium, albeit to lower levels compared to wild type (Figure 3H,I and K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3H,I,K.

claim: nhr-49/PPARA is essential for the induction of fmo-2/FMO5 in the entire body.
source: Thus, nhr-49/PPARA appeared to be essential for the induction of fmo-2/FMO5 in the entire body.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fluorescence microscopy data comparing wild type, hlh-30, and nhr-49 mutants.

claim: Noninfected nhr-49/PPARA mutants exhibited about 10-fold lower fmo-2/FMO5 expression than wild type by RT-qPCR.
source: Consistently, noninfected nhr-49/PPARA mutants exhibited about 10-fold lower fmo-2/FMO5 expression than wild type by RT-qPCR (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: After infection, nhr-49/PPARA mutants completely failed to induce fmo-2/FMO5.
source: After infection, nhr-49/PPARA mutants completely failed to induce fmo-2/FMO5 (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Transgenic rescue of nhr-49/PPARA driven by its endogenous promoter partially restored fmo-2/FMO5 induction.
source: Transgenic rescue of nhr-49/PPARA driven by its endogenous promoter partially restored fmo-2/FMO5 induction (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: nhr-49/PPARA is absolutely required for fmo-2/FMO5 expression in infected and noninfected animals.
source: Therefore, nhr-49/PPARA was absolutely required for fmo-2/FMO5 expression in infected and noninfected animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RT-qPCR and fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: Only K08C7.4 induction by S. aureus was also dependent on NHR-49/PPAR-α among the other five HLH-30-independent genes.
source: RT-qPCR of the other five HLH-30-independent genes showed that only K08C7.4 induction by S. aureus was also dependent on NHR-49/PPAR-α (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: nhr-49/PPARA null mutants showed defective survival of S. aureus infection compared to wild type.
source: Compared to wild type, nhr-49/PPARA null mutants showed defective survival of S. aureus infection (Figure 4A) and shorter lifespan when fed nonpathogenic E. coli (Figure 4B), as previously reported (Van Gilst et al., 2005), suggesting that NHR-49/PPAR-α may have important roles in both host defense and aging.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 4A, with a citation to Van Gilst et al., 2005.

claim: nhr-49/PPARA null mutants showed shorter lifespan when fed nonpathogenic E. coli.
source: Compared to wild type, nhr-49/PPARA null mutants showed defective survival of S. aureus infection (Figure 4A) and shorter lifespan when fed nonpathogenic E. coli (Figure 4B), as previously reported (Van Gilst et al., 2005), suggesting that NHR-49/PPAR-α may have important roles in both host defense and aging.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by lifespan assay data shown in Figure 4B, with a citation to Van Gilst et al., 2005.

claim: Transgenic rescue of nhr-49/PPARA driven by its endogenous promoter completely rescued the infection survival defect.
source: Transgenic rescue of nhr-49/PPARA driven by its endogenous promoter completely rescued the infection survival defect (Figure 4A) but only partially restored the total lifespan on E. coli (Figure 4B), suggesting that distinct thresholds of NHR-49/PPAR-α function exist in infection and aging.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Transgenic rescue of nhr-49/PPARA driven by its endogenous promoter only partially restored the total lifespan on E. coli.
source: Transgenic rescue of nhr-49/PPARA driven by its endogenous promoter completely rescued the infection survival defect (Figure 4A) but only partially restored the total lifespan on E. coli (Figure 4B), suggesting that distinct thresholds of NHR-49/PPAR-α function exist in infection and aging.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by lifespan assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Distinct thresholds of NHR-49/PPAR-α function exist in infection and aging.
source: Transgenic rescue of nhr-49/PPARA driven by its endogenous promoter completely rescued the infection survival defect (Figure 4A) but only partially restored the total lifespan on E. coli (Figure 4B), suggesting that distinct thresholds of NHR-49/PPAR-α function exist in infection and aging.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential rescue of infection survival and lifespan by the same transgene.

claim: Two distinct nhr-49/PPARA gain-of-function mutants showed enhanced infection survival relative to wild type.
source: Moreover, relative to wild type, two distinct nhr-49/PPARA gain-of-function mutants (Lee et al., 2016; Svensk et al., 2013) showed enhanced infection survival (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 4C, with citations to Lee et al., 2016 and Svensk et al., 2013.

claim: Gain-of-function mutant nhr-49(et7) (gf1) exhibited prolonged lifespan on E. coli.
source: In contrast, gain-of-function mutant nhr-49(et7) (gf1) exhibited prolonged lifespan on E. coli, while nhr-49(et8) (gf2) exhibited shortened lifespan (Figure 4D), consistent with previous results (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by lifespan assay data shown in Figure 4D, with a citation to Lee et al., 2016.

claim: Gain-of-function mutant nhr-49(et8) (gf2) exhibited shortened lifespan on E. coli.
source: In contrast, gain-of-function mutant nhr-49(et7) (gf1) exhibited prolonged lifespan on E. coli, while nhr-49(et8) (gf2) exhibited shortened lifespan (Figure 4D), consistent with previous results (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by lifespan assay data shown in Figure 4D, with a citation to Lee et al., 2016.

claim: NHR-49/PPAR-α promotes host infection survival.
source: These results showed that NHR-49/PPAR-α promotes host infection survival, while its function in aging may be more complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the survival and lifespan assay data for nhr-49 loss-of-function and gain-of-function mutants.

claim: The function of NHR-49/PPAR-α in aging may be more complex than its function in host infection survival.
source: These results showed that NHR-49/PPAR-α promotes host infection survival, while its function in aging may be more complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of nhr-49 gain-of-function alleles on lifespan.

claim: Noninfected nhr-49/PPARA gain-of-function mutants exhibited constitutively elevated fmo-2/FMO5 expression relative to wild type by RT-qPCR.
source: Also in line with previous results (Lee et al., 2016), RT-qPCR of noninfected animals showed constitutively elevated fmo-2/FMO5 expression in gain-of-function nhr-49/PPARA mutants relative to wild type (Figure 4E), consistent with the observed pro-survival function of NHR-49/PPAR-α.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4E, with a citation to Lee et al., 2016.

claim: Upon infection, both nhr-49/PPARA gain-of-function mutants exhibited further fmo-2/FMO5 induction, reaching higher fmo-2/FMO5 expression than wild type controls.
source: Upon infection, both gain-of-function mutants exhibited further fmo-2/FMO5 induction, reaching higher fmo-2/FMO5 expression than wild type controls (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: On nonpathogenic E. coli, nhr-49/PPARA gain-of-function mutants exhibited constitutively high fmo-2/FMO5 reporter GFP expression in the anterior pharynx, pharyngeal isthmus, nervous system, and the intestinal epithelium.
source: Consistently, on nonpathogenic E. coli nhr-49/PPARA gain-of-function mutants exhibited constitutively high fmo-2/FMO5 reporter GFP expression in the anterior pharynx, pharyngeal isthmus, nervous system, and the intestinal epithelium (Figure 4F,H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4F,H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Infection further increased fmo-2/FMO5 reporter expression throughout the body in nhr-49/PPARA gain-of-function mutants, becoming much stronger than wild-type animals.
source: Infection further increased reporter expression throughout the body in nhr-49/PPARA gain-of-function mutants, becoming much stronger than wild-type animals (Figure 4G,I,J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4G,I,J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: nhr-49/PPARA activation is sufficient for fmo-2/FMO5 expression in a spatially restricted pattern.
source: These results suggested that nhr-49/PPARA activation is sufficient for fmo-2/FMO5 expression in a spatially restricted pattern, and confirmed that infection synergistically upregulates fmo-2/FMO5 expression throughout the entire body.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nhr-49 gain-of-function mutants show constitutive fmo-2 expression in specific tissues.

claim: Infection synergistically upregulates fmo-2/FMO5 expression throughout the entire body.
source: These results suggested that nhr-49/PPARA activation is sufficient for fmo-2/FMO5 expression in a spatially restricted pattern, and confirmed that infection synergistically upregulates fmo-2/FMO5 expression throughout the entire body.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that infection further increases fmo-2 expression in nhr-49 gain-of-function mutants.

claim: nhr-49/PPARA is expressed in multiple tissues.
source: nhr-49/PPARA is expressed in multiple tissues (Ratnappan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ratnappan et al., 2014.

claim: Intestinal rescue of nhr-49/PPARA fully restored both basal and induced fmo-2/FMO5 expression.
source: Intestinal rescue of nhr-49/PPARA fully restored both basal and induced fmo-2/FMO5 expression (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Re-expression of nhr-49/PPARA in neurons, muscle, or epidermis partially restored fmo-2/FMO5 induction.
source: Re-expression of nhr-49/PPARA partially restored fmo-2/FMO5 induction in other lines (Figure 5D,G,J).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5D,G,J.

claim: Intestinal, neuronal, and muscular expression of nhr-49/PPARA enhanced infection survival compared to wild type.
source: In fact, intestinal, neuronal, and muscular expression enhanced infection survival compared to wild type (Figure 5B,E,H), while epidermal expression rescued infection survival to a level similar to wild type (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 5B,E,H.

claim: Epidermal expression of nhr-49/PPARA rescued infection survival to a level similar to wild type.
source: In fact, intestinal, neuronal, and muscular expression enhanced infection survival compared to wild type (Figure 5B,E,H), while epidermal expression rescued infection survival to a level similar to wild type (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: nhr-49/PPARA can function from intestine, neurons, muscle, or epidermis to promote host defense against infection.
source: These results suggested that nhr-49/PPARA can function from any of these tissues to promote host defense against infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tissue-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Intestinal and epidermal re-expression of nhr-49/PPARA prolonged lifespan compared to wild type.
source: Intestinal and epidermal re-expression prolonged lifespan compared to wild type (Figure 5C,L).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by lifespan assay data shown in Figure 5C,L.

claim: Neuronal expression of nhr-49/PPARA rescued lifespan to the wild-type level.
source: Neuronal expression rescued lifespan to the wild-type level (Figure 5F), and muscle expression yielded partial rescue (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by lifespan assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Muscle expression of nhr-49/PPARA yielded partial rescue of lifespan.

source: These results are consistent with a model in which hlh-30/TFEB and nhr-49/PPARA function in parallel pathways for longevity, while they function in the same pathway for infection survival.

Therefore, hlh-30/TFEB deletion completely suppressed the enhanced survival phenotypes of nhr-49/PPARA gain-of-function alleles, which is consistent with hlh-30/TFEB functioning downstream of nhr-49/PPARA for host infection survival.

claim: hlh-30/TFEB functions downstream of nhr-49/PPARA for host infection survival.
source: Therefore, hlh-30/TFEB deletion completely suppressed the enhanced survival phenotypes of nhr-49/PPARA gain-of-function alleles, which is consistent with hlh-30/TFEB functioning downstream of nhr-49/PPARA for host infection survival.

source: In contrast, both double mutants showed increased lifespan on nonpathogenic E. coli compared to hlh-30/TFEB single mutants (Figure 7D), suggesting that nhr-49PPARA functions downstream of, or parallel to, hlh-30/TFEB for lifespan determination.

claim: hlh-30/TFEB is only partially required for fmo-2/FMO5 expression.
source: Because hlh-30/TFEB mutation did not fully suppress either gain-of-function allele, for the fmo-2/FMO5 expression phenotype hlh-30/TFEB and nhr-49/PPARA appear to function in parallel (additive) pathways and thus, hlh-30/TFEB is only partially required for fmo-2/FMO5 expression.

claim: The host response to S. aureus infection is not entirely the result of starvation.

claim: HLH-30/TFEB integrates metabolic and other stresses to contribute to stress-specific transcriptional responses.

claim: NHR-49/PPAR-α has a novel role in host defense against S. aureus infection.

claim: Enterococcus faecalis induces fmo-2/FMO5 during infection of C. elegans.

claim: NHR-49/PPAR-α appears to play an important role in defense against a broad range of bacteria.
